title: Build commands, compiler flags, warnings and language-standard selection (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the stages of a hosted C build and distinguish source files, object files, libraries and executables.
Select an explicit C language standard and explain strict conformance options versus compiler extensions.
Use warning flags to expose suspicious conversions, shadowing and non-portable constructs.
Distinguish compile diagnostics, linker failures and runtime failures using command output.
Construct repeatable single-file and multi-file build commands with explicit inputs and outputs.
Document compiler identity, version, flags and target environment for reproducible builds.

understand.concept: A build command selects the compiler, language standard, warning options, include paths, source files, object files, libraries and linker inputs. The compiler driver coordinates preprocessing, compilation, assembly and linking.
understand.whyItMatters: Identical source can behave differently under different standards, extensions, warning settings, libraries or targets. Explicit build settings improve portability and reproducibility.
understand.analogy: A build configuration is a documented contract between source code and the toolchain.
understand.analogyLimit: Compiler flags are implementation-specific; one compiler's options are not universal.

explain.narrative: Use an explicit mode such as -std=c17 or -std=c23 when supported. Compiler defaults may change and may enable extensions. GCC/Clang-style -pedantic requests diagnostics for some non-standard extensions. Common warning options include -Wall, -Wextra and -Wpedantic; -Wconversion and -Wshadow add further diagnostics on supported compilers. Treat -Werror as a deliberate project policy after the warning baseline is understood. A one-command build can compile and link multiple sources. For larger projects, compile each source to an object with -c, then link the objects. Include paths are often supplied with -I. Syntax/type diagnostics occur during compilation; undefined references usually occur during linking; crashes and wrong results occur at runtime. Record compiler name/version, target, standard, flags, dependencies and exact commands.

examples.title: Build a single source with explicit diagnostics
examples.explanation: The command selects C17, warning groups, debug symbols and a debug-oriented optimization level. Verify option support with the selected compiler.

examples.title: Compile and link separate translation units
examples.explanation: Each source is compiled to an object file, then the linker resolves the external function reference. A real project should put the shared declaration in a header.

practise.guidedTask: Build a small program with an explicit standard and warning flags. Record the exact command and identify compiler-specific options.
practise.independentTask: Create a reproducible build note for a two-file C program: compiler/version, target, standard, warnings, compile commands, link command and expected output. Introduce a missing function definition and identify the link-stage diagnostic.
hints: Set the language standard explicitly instead of relying on compiler defaults.
-Wall and -Wextra enable useful warning groups but do not detect every defect.
-Wpedantic, -Wconversion and -Wshadow behaviour depends on the compiler.
Use -Werror only as a deliberate policy after understanding the warning baseline.
-c compiles a translation unit without linking an executable.
Record compiler version, flags, target and commands for reproducibility.

questions.prompt: Why specify a C standard with a compiler option?
options: To make the intended language version explicit instead of relying on a compiler default.
questions.answer: To make the intended language version explicit instead of relying on a compiler default.
questions.explanation: Defaults and extension modes can change between compiler versions.

questions.prompt: What does -c do in common GCC/Clang-style drivers?
options: Compiles a source file to an object file without linking an executable.
questions.answer: Compiles a source file to an object file without linking an executable.
questions.explanation: The object file can be linked with other objects and libraries later.

questions.prompt: What is a likely cause of an undefined reference diagnostic?
options: A missing or mismatched definition discovered during linking.
A missing semicolon always discovered by the linker.
questions.answer: A missing or mismatched definition discovered during linking.
questions.explanation: The linker cannot resolve a referenced external symbol.

questions.prompt: What should happen before adding -Werror to a project?
options: Understand and stabilize the warning baseline, then adopt it as an explicit policy.
Assume every compiler emits identical warnings.
questions.answer: Understand and stabilize the warning baseline, then adopt it as an explicit policy.
questions.explanation: -Werror turns warnings into errors and can make builds sensitive to compiler-version changes.

questions.prompt: Which information best supports a reproducible build?
options: Compiler/version, target, language standard, flags, dependencies and exact commands.
questions.answer: Compiler/version, target, language standard, flags, dependencies and exact commands.
questions.explanation: Reproduction requires the toolchain and material configuration choices.
